check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and confirms the identity of the child and parent.
Empathic, non-judgemental approach that acknowledges the parent's frustration and does not blame them for the delay.
Uses plain language with Linh and checks understanding.
History
Characterises the cough:

kids.x: Nature, timing and triggers (dry then wet, day and night, no trigger).
Noisy breathing or localised wheeze (occasional right-sided noise).

check.x: Asks specifically about a sudden onset, choking, gagging or an event while eating or playing with small objects:

kids.x: Elicits the witnessed choking episode at a party after eating mixed nuts five weeks ago.
Establishes that the cough began that same evening.

check.x: Reviews previous treatments and response (amoxicillin, prednisolone and salbutamol, no response).
Asks about access to small objects at home and in day care (sibling's Lego and beads).
Screens for other causes of persistent cough:

kids.x: Atopy, eczema, family history of asthma and previous wheeze.
Recurrent chest infections, poor growth, sick contacts, TB contact, smoke exposure.

check.x: Screens for upper airway and deep neck infection red flags: fever, drooling, difficulty swallowing, neck stiffness or head tilt, stridor, voice change (all absent).
Asks about feeding, hydration, wet nappies, growth, immunisations and development.
Explores Linh's concerns and expectations (feels fobbed off, worried something has been missed).
Examination
General inspection from a distance: alertness, colour, drooling, stridor, voice, head tilt, cyanosis.
Assesses work of breathing and asks for respiratory rate, SpO2, heart rate and temperature.
Checks the hands for clubbing, capillary refill and hydration, and plots weight on a growth chart.
Examines the chest, comparing the two sides:

kids.x: Expansion, and the position of the trachea and apex beat (shifted to the right).
Auscultation (reduced air entry and a localised monophonic wheeze at the right base).

check.x: Looks at the throat without a tongue depressor, checks neck movement and swelling, and examines the ears.
Interpretation
Interprets the chest X-ray as right lower lobe collapse with volume loss and mediastinal shift to the right (not simple pneumonia), matching the right-sided signs on examination.
Interprets the observations: mild tachypnoea, SpO2 96%, no fever, stable now, but the airway risk remains.

Links the sudden onset after choking, the failure of antibiotics, steroids and bronchodilators, the localised signs and the X-ray to a likely inhaled foreign body, and explains that no object on the X-ray does not exclude it (nuts are radiolucent).
Considers other causes (pneumonia, asthma, protracted bacterial bronchitis, TB) and why they fit less well.
Explains why retropharyngeal infection is dangerous:

kids.x: The retropharyngeal space runs from the skull base to about T1 to T2 and opens into the superior mediastinum, so infection can spread to cause mediastinitis.
Abscess is most common in young children after a pharyngeal, tonsillar or upper respiratory tract infection.

check.x: Management
Arranges urgent referral to a paediatric centre with paediatric respiratory or ENT services for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia, both to confirm and to remove the foreign body.
Advises nil by mouth pending the anaesthetic and arranges safe transfer: phones the receiving team, and escalates to ambulance transport if there is any deterioration.
Stops further empirical antibiotics, steroids and bronchodilators, explaining why they have not helped.
Explains the diagnosis and plan to Linh and answers honestly: bronchoscopy is the usual and effective treatment, and delay is common because the choking event is often missed.

Outlines the urgent approach to a suspected retropharyngeal abscess: keep the child calm, avoid distressing examination of the throat, secure the airway with senior, anaesthetic and ENT help, obtain imaging (CT neck with contrast) once safe, start IV antibiotics and involve ENT for possible drainage.
Safety netting
Tells Linh to call 000 for sudden worsening: noisy breathing (stridor), hard or fast breathing, blue colour, or complete choking.
Gives choking first aid for a toddler: encourage coughing if it is effective; if not, back blows and chest thrusts and call 000. No blind finger sweeps.

Counsels on prevention without blame: no whole nuts or hard, small or round foods under 5 years, keep small objects and toy parts (the sibling's Lego and beads) away, and keep children seated and supervised while eating.
Arranges follow-up: GP review after the bronchoscopy to check the cough has settled and the lung has re-expanded, and sooner if the cough returns.

desc: This station involves a focused history from the parent and a focused examination of a toddler with a five-week cough that has not responded to antibiotics, steroids or bronchodilators, then interpreting the observations and a chest X-ray showing right lower lobe collapse, outlining urgent management of a likely inhaled foreign body with safety netting, and answering a question on retropharyngeal abscess.
explain:
Inhaled foreign body in a toddler

Foreign body aspiration peaks between one and three years of age, when children explore with their mouths, are not yet able to chew hard foods well, and are often walking, playing or laughing while eating. Nuts, seeds, raw vegetables and small toy parts are common. After the choking event, which may be brief and unwitnessed, many children settle and appear well, so the diagnosis is often delayed.

Think of an inhaled foreign body in a child with a persistent cough that does not respond to antibiotics, steroids or bronchodilators, especially when there is focal collapse on chest X-ray. Other clues are a sudden onset, unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry on one side and recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude aspiration. Many foreign bodies, particularly organic ones such as nuts, are radiolucent.

  • Typical findings include focal collapse or air trapping (hyperinflation) distal to the object.

  • The definitive management is rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia in a centre with paediatric airway expertise.

  • Treatment with antibiotics or bronchodilators will not fix the problem and delays the diagnosis. Prolonged retention risks infection, bronchiectasis and a lung that does not re-expand.

The child should be kept nil by mouth, monitored closely and transferred safely. Parents should know to call 000 if complete obstruction, stridor or severe respiratory distress occurs, and how to give choking first aid. Prevention includes avoiding whole nuts and other hard or small foods under five years, supervising meals and keeping small objects away.

Interpreting the Part 2 results

Jasper's observations show mild tachypnoea and a SpO2 of 96% in a well, afebrile child: stable now, but a foreign body can move and obstruct a larger airway at any time. The chest X-ray shows right lower lobe collapse with volume loss and shift of the mediastinum towards the collapse, which matches the dullness, reduced air entry, monophonic wheeze and tracheal shift found on examination. The absence of a visible object does not exclude an inhaled foreign body, because nuts are radiolucent.

Retropharyngeal space infection

The retropharyngeal space runs from the skull base to about T1 to T2 and opens into the superior mediastinum. Infection here can spread downwards to cause mediastinitis, which is life-threatening. Swelling in the posterior pharynx can also narrow the airway.

Retropharyngeal abscess is most common in young children after a pharyngeal, tonsillar or upper respiratory tract infection. It should be considered when a toddler has fever, sore throat or refusal to swallow, drooling, muffled voice, neck stiffness or torticollis, and sometimes stridor.

  • Keep the child calm and avoid distressing examination. Prioritise airway.

  • Obtain imaging, usually CT neck with contrast, once the child is stable.

  • Start IV antibiotics and involve ENT and anaesthetics for possible drainage.

  • Further complications include jugular vein thrombosis, carotid involvement and aspiration of pus.
focus: Toddler with persistent cough and airway infection
guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2 the examiner hands over the observations and chest X-ray report and asks the questions in order; the last question is about a different child.

A high-performing candidate recognises early that a persistent cough with a treatment-resistant course needs an explanation beyond infection or asthma. They ask about a sudden onset and choking, uncover the nut aspiration without leading the parent, find the right-sided signs and tracheal shift on examination and link them to the X-ray. They arrange urgent referral for rigid bronchoscopy, keep Jasper nil by mouth, give specific safety netting and choking first aid, and counsel on food and toy safety without blame. On retropharyngeal abscess they explain the anatomy (skull base to T1 to T2, continuous with the superior mediastinum), name mediastinitis and airway obstruction as the dangers, and describe airway-first management.

A borderline candidate takes a general cough history but does not ask about choking or a sudden onset, examines the chest without comparing sides, and may suggest more antibiotics, a different inhaler or a repeat X-ray. They may recognise the collapse but not name a foreign body, refer without urgency or fasting, or know that retropharyngeal abscess is serious without being able to say why.
patient:
Role: You are Linh Nguyen, parent of Jasper, aged 2 years 4 months. You are tired and worried, and feel you have been "fobbed off" by earlier clinics. Jasper is with you, playing on the floor. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. Not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

Opening line: "Jasper has had this cough every day for five weeks and nothing is working."

Volunteer freely:

  • The cough is there day and night, sometimes dry and sometimes a bit wet and rattly.
  • It has not improved at all with three treatments from other clinics: a week of amoxicillin, three days of prednisolone liquid, and a puffer with a spacer.
  • You are frustrated and worried that something has been missed.

Only if specifically asked about how it started, choking, gagging or what Jasper was eating:

  • The cough began suddenly five weeks ago at a family birthday party. Jasper was walking around with a handful of mixed nuts from a bowl, then started gagging and coughing and went red in the face for about a minute.
  • It settled by itself, nothing was seen to come out, and you assumed the nuts were swallowed. You did not mention this to the other doctors because Jasper "seemed fine afterwards". The cough started that evening.
  • If the candidate is empathic and asks about it, say: "I honestly never thought it could have gone down the wrong way."

Cough (give when asked):

  • Not worse at any particular time and not triggered by cold air or exercise.
  • No whooping, no vomiting after coughing, no blue episodes since the first event.
  • Only if asked about wheeze or noisy breathing: occasional noisy breathing on the right side of the chest that you can hear with your ear against Jasper's back.

Other symptoms (give when asked):

  • No fever apart from a mild temperature (up to 37.8 °C) on a few days. No night sweats.
  • Eating and drinking normally, weight steady. No drooling. No difficulty or pain with swallowing.
  • No neck pain, stiffness or head tilt. No stridor. No voice change. Normal wet nappies.

Past history:

  • Born at term, no complications, no breathing problems as a newborn.
  • No previous chronic cough, no recurrent chest infections, no hospital admissions.
  • No eczema, food allergy or family history of asthma. No wheeze before this illness.
  • Immunisations up to date. Development normal. No regular medicines, no allergies.
  • No known sick contacts. No travel. No TB contact.

Social history:

  • Lives with both parents and a five-year-old sibling who plays with small Lego pieces and beads.
  • Attends family day care two days a week.
  • Nobody smokes or vapes at home.

Questions to ask the candidate (if not covered):

  • "Why did the antibiotics and puffer not work?"
  • "Will Jasper need to go to hospital? Will they need an operation?"
  • "Is there anything I should have done when it happened?"

Interrupt politely if the candidate uses jargon a parent would not understand.
points: A toddler with persistent cough unresponsive to antibiotics, steroids and inhalers, plus focal collapse, may have an inhaled foreign body needing bronchoscopy.
Always ask about a sudden onset or choking episode; the event is often brief, forgotten or not mentioned.
A normal chest X-ray does not exclude an inhaled foreign body, as many are radiolucent.
The definitive treatment is rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia at a paediatric centre; keep the child fasted and give clear safety-netting.
The retropharyngeal space runs from the skull base to about T1 to T2 and opens into the superior mediastinum, so infection can cause mediastinitis and airway obstruction.
Retropharyngeal abscess is most common in young children after pharyngeal, tonsillar or upper respiratory infection.

stem: You are a GP. Linh Nguyen has brought in Jasper, aged 2 years 4 months, with a daily cough for five weeks that has not got better. A chest X-ray was requested at the last visit and the report has been sent to you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Linh, including any cause for the cough that has not yet been found, and perform a focused examination of Jasper, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Jasper's observations and the chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer the examiner's questions (5 minutes).
title: Persistent cough in a toddler not responding to treatment

part2.lead: Here are Jasper's observations today and the report of the chest X-ray requested at the last visit.

handover.label: Observations today
handover.result: Height not measured today; weight 13 kg, about the 50th centile.

rows.note: Alert and playful on the floor. Intermittent cough. No recession, no stridor.
Repeated at rest on Linh's lap at the end of the consultation.

handover.model:
Written out, not charted: a GP visit has no observation chart. Afebrile (37.4 °C), HR 124 and then 118, normal for age, and CRT under 2 s. RR 32 is mildly fast for a 2-year-old at rest (about 25 to 30 is usual) with no recession or stridor, and SpO2 96% in room air is low-normal; the repeat at rest is much the same. Weight 13 kg on the 50th centile: growth is unaffected.

A well, afebrile child with mild tachypnoea and borderline saturation fits one collapsed lobe, not sepsis or an acute pneumonia. He is stable now, so an urgent same-day transfer can be arranged by phone with the receiving team, but a foreign body can move and block a larger airway: stridor, distress, a falling SpO2 or complete choking means 000 and an ambulance.

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: Chest X-ray, single frontal (AP) view.

Clinical details: 2-year-old with a daily cough for 4 weeks, not improved with amoxicillin, oral prednisolone or salbutamol. ?Pneumonia ?other cause.

Comparison: None.

Findings:

  • Technique: adequate inspiration, not rotated.
  • Trachea and mediastinum: shifted slightly to the right.
  • Right lung: triangular opacity at the right base medially, behind the heart, with loss of the outline of the medial right hemidiaphragm. The right heart border is preserved. The right hilum is lowered. No air bronchograms. The rest of the right lung is clear.
  • Left lung: clear and well expanded. No hyperinflation.
  • Pleura: no pleural effusion, no pneumothorax.
  • Heart: normal size.
  • No radio-opaque foreign body in the neck, airways or chest.
  • Bones and soft tissues: normal.

Conclusion: Right lower lobe collapse with volume loss and shift of the mediastinum to the right. No pleural effusion, no focal consolidation elsewhere and no radio-opaque foreign body. Lobar collapse in a toddler with a persistent cough raises the possibility of an obstructed bronchus; please correlate clinically.
handover.model:
A systematic read: an adequate frontal film; trachea and mediastinum shifted to the right; a triangular opacity at the right base behind the heart, with the medial right hemidiaphragm lost, the right heart border preserved and the right hilum lowered: right lower lobe collapse with volume loss. The left lung is clear, there is no effusion and no radio-opaque foreign body.

It matches the right-sided signs (reduced expansion, dullness, reduced air entry, a monophonic wheeze and tracheal shift to the right), and with the choking episode on nuts and five weeks of cough that did not respond to antibiotics, steroids or salbutamol it points to an inhaled foreign body blocking the right lower lobe bronchus. Nuts are radiolucent, so a film with no visible object does not exclude it. It is not simple pneumonia: the lobe has lost volume, there are no air bronchograms, and antibiotics did not help.

It changes the plan: urgent referral for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia, nil by mouth, and no more antibiotics, steroids or inhalers.
